cards.explanation: The answer is all of them. The text says Sennacherib, king of Assyria, "…attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah." Not most of them, not the good ones. All. That's not a few cookies off the tray, friends, that's the whole tray gone.

The answer is Jerusalem. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian royal officer, is sent "…to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem." Hezekiah is king of Judah, and Jerusalem is where he is. On the way, the Rabshakeh stops by the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer's Field.

The answer is what Hezekiah's confidence is based on. The Rabshakeh opens with, "What is the basis of this confidence of yours?" He starts by poking at what Hezekiah is standing on, friends. Everything else he says builds from that one question.

The word is empty. The Rabshakeh says, "You claim to have a strategy and strength for war, but these are empty words." Notice that's his opinion of Hezekiah's plans. He's the one talking, and he's talking big.

The answer is Egypt. The Rabshakeh says, "Look now, you are trusting in Egypt…" He goes on to say that's what Pharaoh king of Egypt is to all who trust in him. Egypt is the name he puts on the table, friends.

The answer is a splintered reed of a staff. That's his picture, friends. He calls Egypt "…that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it." Picture grabbing a cane for support and it snaps in your palm. That's not a good morning.

The answer is True. The Rabshakeh says Hezekiah removed the high places and altars, "saying to Judah and Jerusalem, ‘You must worship before this altar.’" That's how he tells it, friends. He's using it to knock down the idea of trusting the LORD.

The answer is if they can put riders on them. He says he'll give two thousand horses, "…if you can put riders on them!" That's a gift with a dare stuck on the end, friends. He's saying Judah couldn't even find enough riders.

The answer is True, that's what the Rabshakeh claims. He says, "The LORD Himself said to me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’…" Notice that it's the Rabshakeh saying this about himself, friends.

The answer is wall. The officials say, "Do not speak to us in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall." They ask him to speak Aramaic instead, since they understand it. The Rabshakeh later mentions the men sitting on the wall too.

The answer is False. The officials ask for Aramaic, and the Rabshakeh doesn't give it to them. He asks, "Has my master sent me to speak these words only to you and your master, and not to the men sitting on the wall…" He wants the wall to hear every word, friends.
The answer is True. The text says he "…stood and called out loudly in Hebrew…" That's the very language the officials asked him to avoid, friends. And loud on top of it.

The answer is that the city won't be given to the king of Assyria. The Rabshakeh says Hezekiah tells them, "The LORD will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria." That's the Rabshakeh's report of Hezekiah's words. Right after it he says, "Do not listen to Hezekiah…"

The answer is to eat from his own vine and fig tree. That's his offer, friends. He says, "Make peace with me and come out to me. Then every one of you will eat from his own vine and his own fig tree, and drink water from his own cistern…" It sounds cozy, and he's pitching it hard.
The answer is False. The Rabshakeh says they'll have those things "…until I come and take you away to a land like your own…" The word "until" gives it away, friends. In his plan, they're moved.
The answer is True. After listing the gods, the Rabshakeh asks, "How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?" That's his whole point, friends. He puts the LORD in a list with the others.

The answer is that they stay silent. The text says, "…the people remained silent and did not answer a word…" After all that shouting, nobody says anything back. The reason comes in the same verse: Hezekiah had commanded, "Do not answer him."
The answer is Hezekiah. The people stayed silent because King Hezekiah had commanded, "Do not answer him." The people followed the king's order, friends.

The answer is that they pass on the Rabshakeh's words. The text says Eliakim, Shebna and Joah "…relayed to him the words of the Rabshakeh." They came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn when they did it, friends.
